'''Edward George Gibson''' (born November 8, 1936) is a former [[NASA astronaut]], [[aviator|pilot]], [[engineer]], and [[physicist]].

Before becoming an astronaut, Gibson graduated from the [[University of Rochester]] and the [[California Institute of Technology]]. He became a research assistant in [[jet propulsion]] while completing his studies, and eventually became a research scientist for [[Philco]] Corporation until joining NASA in 1965. Gibson is the last surviving crew member of [[Skylab 4]].

Gibson was selected as part of [[NASA Astronaut Group 4]], the first group of scientist-astronauts. He served on the support crew of [[Apollo 12]], the second Moon landing mission, before working on the development of the [[Skylab]] [[space station]]. In 1973–74, Gibson made his only flight into space as science pilot aboard [[Skylab 4]], the third and final crewed flight to Skylab. He, along with Commander [[Gerald P. Carr|Gerald Carr]] and Pilot [[William R. Pogue|William Pogue]], spent just over 84 days in space.

Gibson resigned from NASA in December 1974, but returned in 1977 to preside over the selection of scientist-astronaut candidates. Gibson retired from NASA for the last time in October 1982.<ref name="Burgess 2006">{{cite book|last1=Burgess|first1=Colin|author-link1=Colin Burgess (author)|title=NASA's Scientist-Astronauts|year=2006|first2=David J.|last2=Shayler|publisher=Springer |bibcode=2006nasa.book.....S|isbn=978-0-387-21897-7}}</ref>{{rp|336}}

==Early life and education==

Gibson was born in [[Buffalo, New York]], on November 8, 1936.<ref name="Burgess 2006" />{{rp|62}} From ages 2 to 8, Gibson battled [[osteomyelitis]]{{mdash}}soft spots in bones{{mdash}}and spent many months in and out of hospitals. Newly-available [[penicillin]] cured the disease. To strengthen his leg that was nearly amputated, Gibson took up sports: swimming, football, and track. He primarily used swimming to strengthen his leg.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/22158625/skylab_3_astronauts_are_welded_together/ |title=Skylab 3 Astronauts are Welded Together by a Single Thread |last=Recer |first=Paul |date=November 23, 1973|via=Newspapers.com |access-date=July 24, 2018|publisher=Greely Daily Tribune|location=Greely, Colorado|agency=Associated Press}}</ref><ref name=leaderpost>{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/28623579/the_leaderpost/|title=One Factor Common to All—Space Rookies|newspaper=The Leader-Post|location=Regina, Saskatchewan|page=11|last1=Recer|first1=Paul|via=Newspapers.com|date=November 19, 1973}}</ref> He was active in the [[Boy Scouts of America]]. He earned the rank of [[First Class Scout (Boy Scouts of America)|First Class]].<ref name="bsa">{{cite web |title=Scouting and Space Exploration |url=http://www.scouting.org/about/factsheets/scouting_space.aspx |publisher=Boy Scouts of America |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303213130/http://www.scouting.org/about/factsheets/scouting_space.aspx |archive-date=March 3, 2016 |url-status=live}}</ref>

Gibson graduated from [[Kenmore West Senior High School|Kenmore Senior High School]] in [[Kenmore, New York]], in 1955, and earned a [[Bachelor of Science]] degree in [[engineering]] from the [[University of Rochester]] in June 1959.<ref name=leaderpost /> At the University of Rochester, Gibson became a member of the [[Theta Chi]] fraternity. He received a [[Master of Science]] degree in engineering ([[jet propulsion]] option) from the [[California Institute of Technology]] (Caltech) in June 1960 and a [[PhD]] in engineering with a minor in [[physics]] from Caltech in June 1964.<ref name=leaderpost /> He was supervised by [[Maria Wonenburger]].

==Early career==
While studying at Caltech, Gibson was a research assistant in the field of [[jet propulsion]] and classical [[physics]]. His technical publications are in the fields of [[plasma physics]] and [[solar physics]]. He was senior research scientist with the Applied Research Laboratories of the [[Philco]] Corporation at [[Newport Beach, California]], from June 1964 until moving to NASA.<ref name=vermontscientist>{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/28637697/the_burlington_free_press/|title=Vermont Scientist May Be On Early Mission to the Moon|newspaper=The Burlington Free Press|location=Burlington, Vermont|date=June 28, 1965|page=1|via=Newspapers.com|agency=Associated Press}}</ref> While at Philco, he did research in [[laser]]s and the [[optics|optical breakdown]] of gases.<ref name="nasabio" />

Gibson has logged more than 4,300 hours flying time—2,270 hours in [[jet aircraft]].<ref name="nasabio" />

==NASA career==
[[File:Skylab4 - February 1974 astronaut Edward Gibson.jpg|thumb|Gibson's spacewalk during his time on Skylab 4]]
Gibson was selected as a [[Astronaut Group 4|scientist-astronaut]] by NASA in June 1965.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/28241336/lebanon_daily_news/|title=Six Young Scientists Become US Astronauts Today at Space Center|agency=UPI|newspaper=Lebanon Daily News|location=Lebanon, Pennsylvania|date=June 29, 1965|page=17|via=Newspapers.com}}</ref> He completed a 53-week course in flight training at [[Williams Air Force Base]], [[Arizona]], and earned his [[United States Air Force|Air Force]] wings. Since then, he has flown [[helicopters]] and the [[T-38 Talon|T-38]].<ref name="nasabio" />

He served as a member of the astronaut support crew and as a [[Flight controller#Spacecraft communicator (CAPCOM)|CAPCOM]] for the [[Apollo 12]] lunar landing,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://history.nasa.gov/SP-4029/Apollo_12a_Summary.htm|title=Apollo by the Numbers: A Statistical Guide|id=SP-4029|publisher=NASA|last1=Orloff|first1=Richard W.|date=June 2004|orig-year=2001}}</ref> becoming the first from the scientist-astronaut group to get a crew assignment of any kind. He also participated in the design and testing of many elements of the [[Skylab]] space station.<ref name="nasabio" />  As part of his preparation for the Skylab program, Gibson studied [[Sun|solar physics]], ultimately writing an introductory monograph/textbook   on solar [[astrophysics]] ''The Quiet Sun'',<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1974/06/30/archives/ed-who-how-do-you-explain-the-fact-that-more-americans-know-who.html|title=Ed Who?|newspaper=The New York Times|last1=Ivins|first1=Molly|date=June 30, 1974}}</ref><ref>{{Cite report |last=Gibson |first=E. G. |date=1973-01-01 |title=The quiet sun |url=https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/19730017119 |language=en}}</ref> apart from 1973 English edition published in the United States there was 1977 [[Russian language|Russian]] edition of this book, published in the [[Soviet Union]]  by [[Mir Publishers]].<ref>{{cite book|title=Astronomy and Astrophysics Abstracts|volume=20|page=34|isbn=9783662123102|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BUntCAAAQBAJ&q=the+quiet+sun+1977+russian+edition&pg=PA34|last1=Böhme|first1=Siegfried|last2=Esser|first2=Ute|last3=Fricke|first3=Walter|last4=Heinrich|first4=Inge|last5=Krahn|first5=Dietlinde|last6=Schmadel|first6=Lutz D.|last7=Zech|first7=Gert|date=March 14, 2013|publisher=Springer }}</ref>

===Skylab 4===
{{Main|Skylab 4}}
[[File:Gibson przy ATM.jpg|thumb|left|Gibson at the [[Apollo Telescope Mount]] console in the Skylab Multiple Docking Adapter]]
Gibson was the science pilot of [[Skylab 4]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/28633661/redlands_daily_facts/|title=Astronauts Begin Chores in Orbiting Skylab 3|agency=UPI|newspaper=Redlands Daily Facts|location=Redlands, California|date=November 27, 1973|page=1|via=Newspapers.com}}</ref> The third and final crewed visit to the Skylab space station, it launched November 16, 1973, and concluded February 8, 1974.<ref name=winona>{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/28516117/the_winona_daily_news/|title=Skylab Astronauts Return Home Safely|newspaper=The Winona Daily News|location=Winona, Minnesota|date=February 8, 1974|page=1|via=Newspapers.com|agency=Associated Press}}</ref> This was the longest crewed flight (84 days 1 hour 15 minutes) in the history of crewed space exploration at that time. Gibson was accompanied on the record-setting 34.5-million-mile flight by Commander [[Gerald P. Carr]] and Pilot [[William R. Pogue]].<ref name=winona /> They successfully completed 56 experiments, 26 science demonstrations, 15 subsystem detailed objectives, and 13 student investigations during their 1,214 revolutions of the [[Earth]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/28516237/valley_morning_star/|title=City Officials Hear Astronaut Describe Plans|newspaper=Valley Morning Star|date=April 22, 1977|page=1|location=Harlingen, Texas|via=Newspapers.com|last1=Ramsay|first1=Jim}}</ref> They also acquired a wide variety of Earth resources observations data using Skylab's Earth resources experiment package camera and [[sensor array]].<ref name=lancaster /> Dr. Gibson was the crewman primarily responsible for the 338 hours of Apollo Telescope Mount operation, which made extensive observations of solar processes.<ref>"NASA's Scientist-Astronauts," David Shayler and [[Colin Burgess (author)|Colin Burgess]]</ref>

Until the Soviet Union's Soyuz 26 broke the record in March 1978, Gibson and his Skylab 4 teammates held the world record for individual time in space: 2,017 hours 15 minutes 32 seconds.<ref name=lancaster>{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/28623196/lancaster_eaglegazette/|title=Skylab Astronauts End Careers in the Military|newspaper=Lancaster Eagle-Gazette|location=Lancaster, Ohio|date=September 9, 1975|page=17|via=Newspapers.com}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/28628260/tulare_advanceregister/|title=Russians End 96-Day Stay in Space Station|agency=UPI|newspaper=Tulare Advance-Register|location=Tulare, California|date=March 16, 1978|via=Newspapers.com|page=7}}</ref> Gibson logged 15 hours and 22 minutes in three [[extra-vehicular activity|EVAs]] outside the Skylab Orbital Workshop.<ref name="nasabio">{{cite web|url=https://www.nasa.gov/sites/default/files/atoms/files/gibson_edward.pdf |title=Edward Gibson Biography|publisher=NASA|access-date=February 3, 2021|date=December 1993}}</ref> Gibson is the last surviving Skylab 4 crew member (Carr died in 2020, and Pogue died in 2014).

Gibson resigned from NASA in December 1974 to do research on Skylab solar physics data as a senior staff scientist with the Aerospace Corporation of [[Los Angeles, California]]. Beginning in March 1976, he served for one year as a consultant to ERNO Raumfahrttechnik GmbH, in [[West Germany]], on Spacelab design under the sponsorship of a U.S. Senior Scientist Award form the [[Alexander von Humboldt Foundation]]. In March 1977, Gibson returned to the [[Astronaut Office]] astronaut candidate selection and training as Chief of the Scientist-Astronaut Candidates. During his second tenure at NASA, Gibson had hoped to fly on another space station mission due to his experience on Skylab, but at the same time was not keen on flying a [[Space Shuttle]] mission. He served as CAPCOM for STS-1.<ref name="Burgess 2006" />{{rp|513}} Gibson ultimately decided to retire from NASA again on October 31, 1982.<ref name="Burgess 2006" />{{rp|336}}

==Post-NASA career==
From July 1980 to August 1987, Gibson worked for [[TRW Inc.|TRW]] as a project manager at [[Space Park]] in support of [[Space Station Freedom]].<ref>{{cite news
|title=Ed Gibson: From Skylab to Space Station
|newspaper=Sentinel (monthly newspaper for employees)
|date=May 1985
|volume=XXVIII
|number=4
|quote=Gibson, who joined TRW in 1980, is project manager of TRW's space station studies on free-flying platforms and the service, repair and maintenance of spacecraft.
}}</ref><ref>{{cite web
|url=https://www.linkedin.com/in/ed-gibson-8a707b30
|title=Ed Gibson: Experience
|website=[[LinkedIn]]
|access-date=17 February 2024
|quote=TRW, Inc; Jul 1980 - Aug 1987; Redondo Beach, California ... He won and led a support contract to NASA’s [[Goddard Space Flight Center|GSFC]] for definition of Earth-observation satellites and servicing facilities on Space Station Freedom.
}}</ref>

In October 1990, Gibson began his own consulting firm, Gibson International Corp. The firm provides consulting services on program management, market development and space infrastructure design and operations.<ref name="nasabio"/>

He has performed a significant amount of speaking and writing, and published a text book in solar physics, two novels, ''Reach'' (1989)<ref>{{cite book |title=Reach: a novel |last=Gibson|first=Edward G.|year=1989 |publisher=Doubleday |location=New York |isbn= 978-0-385-26150-0|oclc=19127626|url= https://books.google.com/books?id=BiGbAAAACAAJ}}</ref> and ''In the Wrong Hands'' (1992),<ref>
{{cite book |title=In the wrong hands |last=Gibson|first=Edward G.|year=1992 |publisher=Bantam|location=New York |isbn= 978-0-553-29567-2|oclc=25720911|url= https://books.google.com/books?id=ShSSA4zmh2kC}}</ref> and edited ''The Greatest Adventure'', a 1994 compilation of stories and pictures on space missions from many astronauts and cosmonauts around the world.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/28636880/the_sydney_morning_herald/|title=Travellers' Bookshelf|newspaper=The Sydney Morning Herald|location=Sydney, New South Wales|date=October 5, 1995|page=29|via=Newspapers.com}}</ref>

He is the author of Space: Ever Farther, Ever Faster, a book reflecting on the history of space exploration and his experiences aboard Skylab 4 which was published by [[Books LLC|Book Publishers LLC]] in 2025.

==Special honors and awards==
Gibson was awarded a [[National Science Foundation]] Fellowship and the R.C. Baker Fellowship at the California Institute of Technology. He received the [[Johnson Space Center]] Certificate of Commendation (1970).<ref name="nasabio" /> He received the City of [[New York City|New York]] Gold Medal (1974).<ref name="nasabio" /> Gibson, along with the rest of the Skylab astronauts, received the City of Chicago Gold Medal in 1974.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/36369414/the_orlando_sentinel/|title=Chicagoans Host Nine Astronauts|newspaper=The Orlando Sentinel|location=Orlando, Florida|date=March 27, 1974|page=13-A|via=Newspapers.com}}</ref> Gibson received the 1974 FAI [[Yuri Gagarin Gold Medal]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/29930187/the_ottawa_journal/|title=World's Fliers Drop Into Ottawa|last1=Cowan|first1=Cliff|newspaper=The Ottawa Journal|location=Ottawa, Ontario|date=September 22, 1975|page=3|via=Newspapers.com}}</ref> In 1976, he received the U.S. Scientist Prize from the [[Alexander von Humboldt Foundation]], which provided funds to research in West Germany for a year.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/28635018/the_journal_news/|title=Astronaut Awarded Prize|newspaper=The Journal News|location=White Plains, New York|page=5|date=March 19, 1976|via=Newspapers.com|agency=Associated Press}}</ref> He received the JSC Special Achievement Award in 1978.<ref name="nasabio" /> Gibson has also been presented with [[Honorary degree|honorary]] doctorates of science from the University of Rochester and [[Wagner College]] in [[New York City]], both in 1974.<ref name="nasabio" />

The three Skylab astronaut crews were awarded the 1973 [[Robert J. Collier Trophy]] "For proving beyond question the value of man in future explorations of space and the production of data of benefit to all the people on Earth."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://naa.aero/awards/awards-and-trophies/collier-trophy/collier-1970-1979-winners|title=Collier 1970–1979 Recipients|publisher=National Aeronautics Association|access-date=February 9, 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/20455982/the_orlando_sentinel/|title=Collier Trophy at Test Range|newspaper=The Orlando Sentinel|location=Orlando, Florida|date=October 3, 1974|page=21|via=Newspapers.com}}</ref> In 1974, President Nixon presented the Skylab 4 crew with the [[NASA Distinguished Service Medal]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/28239377/playground_daily_news/|title=NASA Fund Drive Backed by Nixon|agency=UPI|date=March 21, 1974|page=2|newspaper=Playground Daily News|location=Fort Walton Beach, Florida|via=Newspapers.com}}</ref>  The [[American Astronautical Society]]'s 1975 Flight Achievement Award was awarded to the Skylab 4 crew.<ref name=tene>{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/28403537/the_tennessean/|title=Former Astronaut to Speak Friday|newspaper=The Tennessean|date=June 29, 1983|page=52|via=Newspapers.com}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://astronautical.org/awards/armstrong/|title=Neil Armstrong Space Flight Achievement Award|publisher=American Astronautical Society|access-date=February 13, 2019}}</ref>  [[Federation Aeronautique Internationale]] awarded the Skylab 4 crew the [[De La Vaulx Medal]] and [[Vladimir Komarov|V. M. Komarov]] Diploma for 1974.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.fai.org/awards?receiver=Gibson|title=FAI Awards|date=October 10, 2017|publisher=FÉDÉRATION AÉRONAUTIQUE INTERNATIONALE|access-date=February 13, 2019}}</ref> Carr accepted the 1975 [[Dr. Robert H. Goddard Memorial Trophy]] from President Ford, awarded to the Skylab astronauts.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/20406167/daily_press/|title=For Praises Astronauts, Space Program|agency=UPI|date=April 12, 1975|location=Newport News|newspaper=Daily Press|page=23|via=Newspapers.com}}</ref> The Skylab 4 crew won the [[AIAA]] Haley Astronautics Award in 1975 "For demonstrated outstanding courage and skill during their record-breaking 84-day Skylab mission".<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.aiaa.org/HonorsAndAwardsRecipientDetails.aspx?recipientId=8f80c1e0-373f-4d0d-b0ae-7e8721302d34|title=Haley Space Flight Award|publisher=AIAA|access-date=February 12, 2019}}</ref> He was one of 24 Apollo astronauts who were inducted into the [[U.S. Astronaut Hall of Fame]] in 1997.<ref>[http://www.astronautscholarship.org/gibson.html Edward G. Gibson] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071008200902/http://www.astronautscholarship.org/gibson.html |date=October 8, 2007 }}, retrieved August 23, 2007</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/28283877/florida_today/|title=Ceremony to Honor Astronauts|newspaper=Florida Today|location=Cocoa, Florida|page=2B|date=October 2, 1997|last1=Meyer|first1=Marilyn|via=Newspapers.com}}</ref>

==Personal life==
[[File:Edward and Julianne Gibson, 1965.jpg|thumb|Edward and Julianne Gibson]]
Gibson is married to Julianne Volk of [[Tonawanda (town), New York|Tonawanda, New York]]. He has four children: Jannet Lynn (born November 9, 1960), John Edward (born May 2, 1964), Julie Ann (born October 12, 1968), and Joseph Michael (born July 11, 1971).<ref>[http://www.spaceacts.com/starship/seh/gibson-e.htm Edward Gibson's family] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170202015530/http://www.spaceacts.com/starship/seh/gibson-e.htm}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/382328625/?terms=edward%20gibson&match=1 |title=A Mother's Prophecy |first=Marvin |last=Miles |newspaper=Los Angeles Times |date=1965-07-02 |via=Newspapers.com |quote=He met the press Thursday, with his attractive wife, Julianne...}}</ref>

== Media appearances ==
In the 1998 [[HBO]] [[miniseries]] ''[[From the Earth to the Moon (miniseries)|From the Earth to the Moon]]'', Gibson was played by actor Geoffrey Nauffts.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0120570/fullcredits?ref_=tt_cl_sm#cast|title=From the Earth to the Moon, Full Cast and Crew|publisher=IMDb|access-date=December 5, 2017}}</ref> As his character serves as Capcom for Apollo 12 regardless of actual shift changes, it can be argued that he is a [[composite character]] of Gibson, [[Gerald Carr (astronaut)| Gerald Carr]], and [[Don Lind]].
